JSON: Name: sie_uprmt_cox7a2l_pipeline Title: Multi-omics and ultrastructural pipeline to test how sprint-interval exercise-induced mitochondrial stress remodels human skeletal muscle mitochondria and respiratory function Short Hypothesis: Acute sprint-interval exercise (SIE) causes transient mitochondrial ultrastructural disruption in human skeletal muscle that activates the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) and the integrated stress response (ISR), increasing COX7A2L incorporation into III+IV supercomplexes and thereby producing a greater training-induced increase in mitochondrial respiratory capacity than matched-volume moderate-intensity continuous exercise (MICE). Related Work: Existing work shows exercise increases mitochondrial biogenesis, respiratory function, and quality-control pathways, and high-intensity interval exercise can produce rapid transcriptional and metabolic responses. Prior studies report exercise-induced increases in PGC-1α and mixed effects on mitochondrial content and function depending on intensity and volume. Animal and in vitro work implicates mitohormesis, UPRmt, ISR and mitophagy in mitochondrial adaptation, and biochemical studies identify COX7A2L as a regulator of III+IV supercomplex assembly under glycolytic conditions. Limitations in the current literature include sparse direct evidence for UPRmt activation in human muscle after acute exercise, few high-resolution ultrastructural (TEM) analyses in humans, inconsistent temporal sampling that misses early transient signals, limited integrated multi-omics linking acute mitochondrial stress to long-term proteome and functional remodeling, and confounding of intensity with volume in training studies. There is also limited causal evidence connecting COX7A2L regulation to exercise-induced respiratory changes in human tissue. Abstract: Problem: It is unresolved how exercise intensity produces distinct mitochondrial adaptations in human skeletal muscle and whether acute high-intensity bouts trigger a mitochondrial-specific stress response that directs long-term remodeling. Approach: Combine a randomized, counterbalanced acute exercise trial (sprint-interval exercise (SIE) versus moderate-intensity continuous exercise (MICE)) with an 8-week parallel training study (SIT versus MICT), integrating time-resolved RNA sequencing, phosphoproteomics, label-free proteomics, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), blue-native PAGE, enzymatic assays, and high-resolution mitochondrial respiration in permeabilized fibers. Main contribution: A defined pipeline that quantifies (1) acute mitochondrial ultrastructural disruption, (2) activation of UPRmt/ISR and mitophagy signaling, (3) COX7A2L abundance and supercomplex redistribution, and (4) how these acute events predict divergence in training-induced respiratory capacity and mitochondrial proteome remodeling; includes in vitro COX7A2L perturbation in human myotubes to test causality. Expected outcome: A validated experimental workflow that determines whether transient SIE-induced mitochondrial stress and UPRmt activation causally reprogram mitochondrial proteostasis and supercomplex assembly to produce greater functional respiratory gains than matched-volume moderate training. Experiments: Cohorts and design: Recruit 28 healthy male adults (target n=14 per group) for acute randomized counterbalanced trial: one session SIE (6×30s all-out sprints, defined load) and one session MICE (continuous cycling ~90–100% LT1, matched session structure as feasible) with muscle biopsies at rest, +0.5h, +1.5h, +3h, +24h. Subset (n≈24, balanced, or 12 per training arm) completes 8-week training: SIT (progressive SIE sessions) vs MICT (progressive MICE sessions); biopsies PRE and 72h POST final session. Measurements: RNA-seq (whole-muscle, paired timepoints) for differential expression and GSEA (FDR<0.05); phosphoproteomics for ISR/MQC phosphosites; label-free shotgun proteomics (LFQ) of whole-muscle and mitochondrial-enriched fractions; TEM quantification (mitochondrial volume density, cristae density/junctions/width, %disturbed mitochondria); BN-PAGE and immunoblot densitometry for COX7A2L and distribution across CI/CIII/CIV assemblies and respirasomes; high-resolution respiration in permeabilized fibers (ETF, ETF+CI, ETF+CI+CII, ETSmax) normalized to wet weight and CS activity; enzymatic assays (CS, complex I activity); immunoblots for eIF2α-pS52, ULK1-pS556, LC3B-II, OPTN-pS177; qPCR for DDIT3, HSPD1, PPP1R15A. Baselines and controls: Resting pre-exercise biopsies as baseline; time-matched blood lactate/ pH monitoring. In vitro ablation/causality: Culture primary human myotubes from matched donors, apply electrical pulse stimulation or metabolic treatments mimicking glycolytic stress vs moderate workload; perform COX7A2L siRNA knockdown and overexpression; measure BN-PAGE SC distribution, respiration (Seahorse or Oroboros), and UPRmt marker induction. Comparisons/ablations: Acute SIE vs MICE time-course (identify early UPRmt/ISR activation); Training SIT vs MICT pre/post changes in mitochondrial proteome and respiration; Correlation and mediation analyses testing whether acute UPRmt/ISR activation or % damaged mitochondria predicts training-induced respiratory gains; In vitro COX7A2L perturbation tests whether COX7A2L is necessary/sufficient for III+IV accumulation and respiration changes under SIE-like metabolic conditions. Statistical analysis: mixed-effects models for repeated measures, FDR correction for multi-omics (q<0.05), pre-specified primary endpoints: mitochondrial volume density, citrate synthase activity, ETF+CI+CII respiration, COX7A2L abundance in III+IV fraction; power calculation based on effect sizes reported (~n=12–14 per arm). Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample and generalizability: limited to healthy young males; findings may not generalize to females, older adults, or clinical populations. Temporal resolution: early transient signals (e.g., UPRmt peak) may occur between sampled timepoints, leading to false negatives. Biological variability: inter-subject heterogeneity in fiber-type composition, diet, circadian rhythm, and prior activity may increase noise and reduce power. Technical: TEM ultrastructure scoring can be subjective and may suffer sampling bias; BN-PAGE resolution may insufficiently separate certain supercomplex assemblies; proteomics dynamic range may miss low-abundance regulatory proteins; phosphoproteomics site coverage may be incomplete. Causality limits: in vitro COX7A2L perturbations in myotubes may not fully recapitulate in vivo multicellular muscle environment and systemic factors. Ethical/feasibility: pharmacological or genetic perturbations in humans are not feasible, limiting direct causal inference in vivo. Statistical/multiplicity: large multi-omics datasets introduce multiple-testing burden and potential false discoveries if not rigorously controlled. Resource/scale: high-resolution TEM, DIA/DDA proteomics, and respiration assays are resource-intensive and may limit cohort size, affecting detection of small effects.
